newsitem.title: USA: RJR Nabisco profits despite Soviet disruptions.
newsitem.headline: RJR Nabisco profits despite Soviet disruptions.

text.p: RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. said Tuesday first-quarter profits rose despite disruptions in tobacco exports to the former Soviet Union and a sales force reorganization in the U.S. biscuit business.

The company, whose products range from Camel cigarettes to Oreo cookies, said net income rose 8 percent to $213 million in the quarter from $198 million in the year-ago period. Earnings per share increased to 62 cents from 57 cents.
Sales edged down 3 percent to $3.78 billion from $3.89 billion.
The company warned, however, that analysts' expectations for the second quarter were too high.
RJR Nabisco said while it was still on track for full-year, per-share net income of $2.99, the consensus estimate of 74 cents per share for the second quarter was too high.
Hunt Whitacre, director of investor relations, said second-quarter net income per share would be closer to 71 cents per share.
Whitacre's comments came during a conference call that was closed to the media. One analyst who was on the call told Reuters of the revision, which was confirmed by the company.
"As a rapidly growing business, we can experience volatility quarter to quarter, but the underlying trends remain very favourable for 1997 and beyond," Chairman Steven Goldstone said in a statement.

Referring to first quarter results, Goldstone said "Overall sales were soft primarily as a result of temporary export disruptions in the former Soviet Union in the tobacco business and the short-term impact of a sales force reorganization in the U.S. Biscuit business which caused some delivery shortfalls during the transition period."

Uncertainty about whether importers in the former Soviet Union had to pay taxes on the cigarettes up front caused them to delay purchases, he said. The import order flow began to return to normal late in the first quarter and tax issues have been clarified.

"We have already put programmes in place to remedy the tobacco volume softness and we remain confident that 1997 will be a very good year in terms of earnings growth and business strengthening," Goldstone said.
For the first quarter, worldwide tobacco sales fell 1 percent from a year ago to $1.87 billion on a volume decline of 9 percent.
Domestic tobacco sales rose 2 percent from the year-ago period to to $1.08 billion. Foreign tobacco sales fell 5 percent to $798 million and volume fell 11 percent.
Camel cigarettes saw good growth in markets such as Greece, Holland, Switzerland, Belgium, Japan, South Africa, and Latin America.
The company's Winston cigarettes division reported solid growth during the quarter in Greece, Turkey, the Adriatic region and Japan.
Salem showed strong performance across Asia, especially in Japan, where Reynolds International continues to be the fastest-growing international tobacco company.
The Biscuit Co. division said U.S. cracker sales edged down, although Air Crisps showed strong gains and cracker profitability rose during the quarter.
In the cookie segment, Oreos reported a strong quarter with sales up 23 percent, although sales softness continued in Newtons and SnackWell's.

The U.S. Foods Group benefited from the successful introduction of SnackWell's Chocolate Candies, the strong growth of Ice Breakers gum, and continuing gains by Planters, which reflects its position as the only nationally branded nut product line, the company said. These gains were offset by lower sales of condiments and table spreads.
RJR Nabisco's major operating companies are R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. and R.J. Reynolds International. RJR Nabisco also owns an 80.5 percent interest in Nabisco Holdings Corp.
RJR Nabisco's stock fell 62.5 cents to $31.75 on the New York Stock Exchange in late trading.
